brief:
The most important development for Printec's competitive position this cycle was a regulatory review, not a lost deal. On **26 August 2026 the UK Competition and Markets Authority formally opened its Phase 1 inquiry** into **Brink's** acquisition of **NCR Atleos**. The legal deadline for a decision is **22 October 2026** ([CMA case page](https://www.gov.uk/cma-cases/the-brinks-company-slash-ncr-atleos-corporation-merger-inquiry)). Atleos has also moved its expected completion date forward to early in the first quarter of 2027.

For Printec the consequence is direct and uncomfortable. The company that supplies the hardware and software behind its whole ATM line is about to change hands. Its new owner is the company competing hardest against Printec's service business. Atleos has said little in the meantime. It held no second-quarter earnings call and published no outlook, and a full-text scan of its release found no mention of Europe or EMEA.

This change of ownership matters because the buyer's strategy is working well. **Brink's** reported second-quarter revenue of USD 1,392m, up 7%. Its ATM managed-services and cash-as-a-service lines, which run ATMs and handle cash for banks as an outsourced service, grew 14% organically ([SEC filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/78890/000007889026000054/exhibit992_2q2026v-micro.htm)).

Europe is where this shift has gone furthest. Revenue there rose only a little, from USD 358m to USD 377m, but margin rose from 16.6% to 18.7%. Brink's is deliberately swapping low-margin cash-in-transit work for high-margin ATM outsourcing, rather than chasing volume.

Brink's announced a new full ATM outsourcing agreement for a European bank consortium, meaning a group of banks. The agreement starts in the second half of the year. It deliberately did not name the country, the banks or the number of machines. In April its ATM managed-services arm shared a stage in Athens with **Mellon** and **KAL**. There it sold full-lifecycle outsourcing directly to decision-makers at National Bank of Greece and Eurobank. That is exactly the revenue Printec earns in its largest market.

Consolidation is also happening closer to Printec's own markets. **Mellon Technologies** filed audited 2025 accounts showing revenue of **EUR 258.8m, up 17%**, with EBITDA up 39% ([group accounts](https://mellongroup.com/assets/uploads/2025_MT_Group_Notes_EN.pdf)). EBITDA means earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. That puts Mellon at roughly Printec's own EBITDA level on about ten times the revenue, so Mellon can absorb a thin-margin bid that Printec cannot.

Four ownership moves disclosed with the accounts matter more than the numbers. Mellon bought Camelot Sistemi in Croatia outright, set up wholly owned companies in Ljubljana and Budapest, and completed the buy-out of Mellon Cyprus. A bidder needs new, funded local subsidiaries before it can win local bank work. **Slovenia, Hungary, Croatia and Cyprus should therefore move from "safe" to "contested"** in account planning.

At the same time, pressure on account-to-account and card payment rails is causing some players to pull back as well as advance. **Payten / Asseco SEE** publicly admitted a retreat in hardware. Its Payment Solutions segment fell 5% to EUR 102.8m, and the ATM line dropped EUR 3.4m on lower deliveries in Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia and Montenegro. This is a reshaping rather than a collapse: group operating profit rose 27%, and contracted margin is rising while contracted revenue falls. A company that takes fewer, better-priced deals is unlikely to buy a tender cheaply this autumn.

**Worldline**'s bank-facing Financial Services division shrank another 7.1% organically to EUR 363m. It booked EUR 60m of contract terminations for the year and expects no return to growth before the second half of 2027. Two convenient assumptions about Worldline should be dropped. In fact its disposal programme is finished, every business it sold sits outside Printec's seventeen countries, and it has not exited ATM management.

**Diebold Nixdorf**'s banking product sales fell 13.0%, and its filing blames lower volumes in the Middle East, Africa and Europe. Even so, it shipped a record number of teller cash recyclers, which are counter machines that re-use deposited notes. It also won a fleet of approximately 1,100 units at a new UK customer, bundled with long-term service. It will run this same replacement approach against NCR-installed banks in Printec's footprint.

Two quieter moves deserve board attention because they attack the business case, not the bid. **KAL** is marketing a Linux virtualisation layer, which is software that lets one operating system run inside another. It lets a newer Windows run on old ATM hardware, even where the hardware vendor no longer supports it. Česká spořitelna is quoted by name saying it can now significantly extend the life of older machines. This is designed to remove the hardware-refresh trigger that Printec's ATM sales depend on.

KAL returns to the Banktech conference in Athens on **8–9 October 2026**, hosted by Mellon. Brink's also holds 13.93% of KAL, which links this directly to the Atleos deal.

In Romania, **PayPoint** and **SelfPay** are doing the same thing from below. They offer cash withdrawal at more than 14,000 assisted point-of-sale locations, heading for 26,000. They also run over 13,000 self-service payment stations, heading for roughly 19,000. This is the cheapest substitute yet for a rural cash machine, and both work against the case for cash-dispensing ATMs.

A 35,000-terminal estate and a 13,000-station estate are also two of the largest managed-services targets in the country. The right first approach to each is as a customer, not a rival.

Among partners and adjacent players, **Glory** had the best quarter of anyone. EMEA revenue rose 27.1% and, for the first time, made up more than half its overseas revenue. Overseas operating margin rose from 5.0% to 8.7%.

Glory also put a date on the next cash-hardware cycle. It told investors that special demand from the **euro banknote redesign** is expected from around 2029. The ECB's public survey on ten shortlisted designs closes on **21 September 2026** ([ECB](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/pr/date/2026/html/ecb.pr260723~c2d43f9170.en.html)). The honest counterweight is that Glory names no CEE or SEE customer anywhere, and says European teller-recycler sales to banks remained weak.

**Euronet**'s Greek deal with CrediaBank had still not closed as at 31 August. It covers buying CrediaBank's merchant-acquiring business and managing its 141 ATMs. Merchant acquiring is card payment processing for shops. It appears nowhere in Euronet's second-quarter filing, and there is no notification on the Hellenic Competition Commission register, against a stated third-quarter target. That makes **30 September a hard decision point**.

Two earlier readings of Euronet were corrected. Its ATM economics are not collapsing, and its estate is essentially flat at 57,071 machines. Its growth now comes from acquiring, issuing and software, not from taking over bank fleets.

Finally, two names joined the tracked set that a 164-vendor list had missed entirely, and both are global tier. **Giesecke+Devrient**'s currency-technology arm holds the high-speed central-bank banknote-sorter tier that Printec's product line does not reach. It has now **won Banka Slovenije's six-year sorter-maintenance contract, awarded 21 August 2026 at EUR 1,890,000 on a single bid**. That locks the tier up until 2032. Its identity joint venture **Veridos** won Cyprus' end-to-end electronic travel-document contract at **EUR 22,900,450** on lowest price.

In Greece, **BOOS S.A.** was absent from the competitor list until this cycle. It won the year's largest Greek counter-cash-automation contract: a five-year operational lease of 300 banknote counting and sorting machines for Hellenic Post. The contract uses Double Power machines rather than Glory. This is a loss on price and lease model, not a change of channel. It also gives BOOS a live public-sector reference to bid against Printec at Greek banks.
